## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. - dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- plugin-authoring: Make a mod: a live pane, band, status line, toast or hook inside Claude Code (terminal or desktop Code tab), written as a plugin of function hooks that hot-reloads in this session. Load before writing or debugging a hooks module.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- anthropic-skills:built-in-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Claude desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Claude's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. - anthropic-skills:chrome-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. - anthropic-skills:deep-research: Use this skill when the user's prompt requires (1) researching a topic across multiple sources, comparing options or alternatives, analyzing trends or history, understanding markets or industries, or reviewing literature or studies and (2) synthesizing that research into a comprehensive, narrative report. schema.name: Bash
schema.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.name: Glob
schema.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

schema.name: Grep
schema.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

1	// Prompts for the spec, builder, and fixer agents. The playtester prompt lives with the game runtime.
2	
3	const TESTABLE = `The playtester controls a real player bot ("@bot") on a local Paper 1.21.4 superflat server with these tools:
4	game_setup(console commands run as the bot; ^ and ~ are relative to it), reset_arena (flat arena, no mobs, empty inventory), bot_state,
5	nearby_entities (id, type, position, velocity, health), attack_sequence(entityIds, intervalTicks, trackTicks) (back-to-back hits in one call, for cooldowns),
6	equip(item), look_at, move_to, attack(entityId, trackTicks), use_item(entityId?, trackTicks),
7	shoot(entityId | entityIds | position, item?, chargeTicks?) (aims and fires a bow, crossbow, trident or throwable; entityIds fires several shots back to back in one call;
8	reports each projectile, every explosion with its position, ammo used, chat, and health before/after, deaths and max velocity of every living entity nearby),
9	track_entity(entityId, ticks) (per-tick position and velocity with maxUpwardVelocity and maxHeightGain), wait_ticks, chat (including /commands), read_chat,
10	server_log (console, including plugin exceptions and the plugin's own getLogger() lines).`;
11	
12	function spec(prompt) {
13	  return `You are the spec agent for Benana Mod Studio. A user described a Minecraft mod. Turn it into a Paper plugin spec and a test plan
14	that an AI playtester can execute in-game and judge with measurements.
15	
16	User's description:
17	"""${prompt}"""
18	
19	${TESTABLE}
20	
21	Rules for the test plan:
22	- 2 to 4 checks. Each check targets one behavior and has an "expect" with a measurable threshold (velocity, height, count, chat text, health).
23	- "setup" holds console commands without a leading slash. Use @bot for the bot. Give the bot the items it needs.
24	- Summon mobs with {PersistenceRequired:1b}. Never use NoAI:1b (NoAI mobs ignore velocity and knockback). Prefer husks to zombies (zombies burn in daylight).
25	- Summon melee targets 2-3 blocks in front of the bot, e.g. "summon husk ^ ^ ^3 {PersistenceRequired:1b}". Summon ranged targets
26	  (bows, tridents, snowballs) 8-12 blocks away, e.g. "summon husk ^ ^ ^10 {PersistenceRequired:1b}", and use the shoot tool, never use_item.
27	- Explosions hit everything nearby. Space mobs that must stay unharmed at least 8 blocks from any blast, and start checks that need a clean
28	  world (fresh mobs, no cooldown left over) with reset_arena followed by their own setup.
29	- Every check must name the tool that produces its measurement. Prefer direct evidence (an explosion position, a health number, a chat line,
30	  a server_log line) over indirect signs such as a mob disappearing.
31	- Timing-sensitive checks (cooldowns) must happen inside ONE tool call: attack_sequence for melee, shoot with entityIds for ranged. Separate
32	  tool calls are several real seconds apart.
33	- Include a check for any limit the user mentioned (cooldowns, permissions, item requirements) and one negative check where it is cheap (for example, a different item does nothing).
34	- Velocity is in blocks per tick. A normal sword hit's knockback gives about 0.4 upward; a strong launch is above 1.0.
35	
36	Respond with ONLY a JSON object, no prose:
37	{
38	  "modName": "PascalCase plugin name, letters only, max 24 chars",
39	  "summary": "one sentence",
40	  "behavior": ["precise behavior bullet", "..."],
41	  "testPlan": {
42	    "version": 1,
43	    "modName": "same as above",
44	    "summary": "same as above",
45	    "setup": ["..."],
46	    "checks": [{ "id": "kebab-case", "title": "...", "steps": "...", "expect": "..." }]
47	  }
48	}`;
49	}
50	
51	function builder({ mod, lessons }) {
52	  return `You are the builder agent for Benana Mod Studio. Implement this Paper plugin in the current repository.
53	
54	Mod: ${mod.name}: ${mod.spec.summary}
55	User's description: """${mod.prompt}"""
56	
57	Behavior:
58	${mod.spec.behavior.map((b) => `- ${b}`).join('\n')}
59	
60	The in-game playtester will run this test plan after you finish (also in playtest/test-plan.json):
61	${JSON.stringify(mod.testPlan.checks, null, 2)}
62	
63	Read CLAUDE.md for the repository conventions. The main class dev.benana.mod.${mod.name} already exists as a stub.
64	${lessons.length ? `\nLessons from earlier mods built in Benana (apply them):\n${lessons.map((l) => `- ${l}`).join('\n')}\n` : ''}
65	Work steps:
66	1. Implement the behavior. Keep it to the Paper API. Log every key action and decision with getLogger().info (for example "X shot an
67	   explosive arrow", "cooldown 3.2s remaining", "explosion at x,y,z"); the playtester reads these lines as evidence.
68	2. Run \`mvn -q package\` and fix every compile error until target/${mod.name}.jar builds.
69	3. Do not commit. Finish with a short summary of what you implemented.`;
70	}
71	
72	function fixer({ mod, attempt, previous, context }) {
73	  const failed = (previous.verdict?.checks || []).filter((c) => c.status !== 'pass');
74	  const evidence = previous.failure?.kind === 'build'
75	    ? `The build failed. Maven output (tail):\n${previous.build?.log?.slice(-4000) || '(none)'}`
76	    : previous.failure?.kind === 'load'
77	      ? `The plugin did not load on the server. Errors:\n${(previous.deploy?.errors || []).join('\n').slice(0, 4000)}`
78	      : `The in-game playtester reported:\n${JSON.stringify({ summary: previous.verdict?.summary, failedChecks: failed, serverErrors: previous.verdict?.serverErrors }, null, 2).slice(0, 8000)}`;
79	  return `You are the fixer agent for Benana Mod Studio. Attempt ${attempt.n - 1} of the ${mod.name} plugin failed. Fix it.
80	
81	Mod: ${mod.name}: ${mod.spec.summary}
82	Behavior:
83	${mod.spec.behavior.map((b) => `- ${b}`).join('\n')}
84	
85	Full test plan: playtest/test-plan.json. Previous verdicts: playtest/attempt-*/verdict.json.
86	
87	${evidence}
88	
89	Repository history (Entire checkpoints link each commit to the agent session that produced it):
90	${context.history || '(none)'}
91	${context.checkpoints ? `\nEntire checkpoints:\n${context.checkpoints}` : ''}
92	${context.trace ? `\nNeatlogs trace of the failed playtest session:\n${context.trace}` : ''}
93	
94	Steps:
95	1. Find the root cause from the evidence; the playtester's measurements are ground truth, and its suspected cause is only a guess.
96	2. Make the smallest change that fixes it. Run \`mvn -q package\` until it builds.
97	3. Do not commit. End your reply with exactly one line:
98	LESSON: <one sentence a future builder should know to avoid this bug>`;
99	}
100	
101	module.exports = { spec, builder, fixer };

content.thinking:
I'm thinking a mod should stay as a single chat thread, with follow-ups treated as additional turns rather than separate mods. That means adding a `turns` array to the mod, where each turn captures its own prompt, timestamp, and starting attempt number, with the first turn representing the original prompt.

For revising, I need a backend handler that requires the mod to be idle with a repo already set up, appends the new turn and feed entry, then runs the spec agent again against the existing spec and test plan plus the change request -- while forcing the mod name to stay fixed so the repo, Maven artifact, and main class don't change. Attempt numbering needs to keep incrementing from the last attempt rather than resetting, since attempt numbers are tied to playtest directories, MCP files, and UI lookups.

I'm also tracking where the code relies on attempt roles or counts -- ResultCard, PipelineChecklist, TestPanel, ModsPage, and the shared verdict/spend/phase helpers -- since adding a "reviser" role as the first attempt of a revise turn (followed by "fixer" attempts) means I need to update all these call sites. I'm also rethinking how the UI thread renders multiple turns, since old mods don't have user feed entries to build a chat bubble from.

For PipelineChecklist specifically, I realize showing it tied to the current mod phase breaks once there are multiple turns, since an earlier turn's checklist would end up reflecting the latest phase instead of its own. The cleanest fix is giving PipelineChecklist an `isLatest` flag so only the newest turn's checklist is live, while earlier turns render as a static, completed summary.

I'm overcomplicating this. Maybe the simplest approach is to only render the full step-by-step checklist for turn one and whichever turn is currently running, and collapse earlier turns into a short one-line summary of their outcome instead of replaying the whole checklist state.

I should check how phaseIndex is computed in shared.jsx and how attempts and end states get tracked across TestPanel.jsx and ModsPage.jsx before deciding how to freeze a turn's displayed state.

For the ResultCard, it makes sense to only render it for the latest finished turn—past turns already get their closure from the "done" phase-line text in the feed, so appending ResultCard just once at the end works naturally. Similarly, I think I'll skip showing PipelineChecklist for past turns and reserve it for the current turn only, letting the phase lines alone narrate history.

But then turn 1's plan card would just vanish once the user follows up, which feels like a regression—history shouldn't disappear visually. A better approach is to freeze the turn's outcome: store something like `turn.endedPhase` at the moment it finishes, then render past checklists as all-done except where a fixer step was skipped, or mark the final step as failed if the turn ended in failure.

There's also the TestPanel to worry about—it reads `mod.testPlan` and `latestVerdict(mod)`. Since the test plan gets replaced after turn 2, old verdicts referencing old check ids could leak stale statuses into the new plan's checklist via the shared `byId` lookup, until a fresh verdict arrives. I should probably scope `latestVerdict` to the current turn, returning null if the latest attempt hasn't produced a verdict yet—need to check how it's implemented in shared.jsx.

I also need to update the welcome placeholder text to reference the open mod's name, keep the "New" button and sidebar "New mod" button, and hide the "Seeded bug" toggle once a mod is open since seeding only applies to fresh mods. The running-dock condition and `canStart` gating during builds both seem fine as-is, as does resetting non-terminal statuses to 'stopped' on restart.

Then there's the trickier case of follow-ups on stopped or failed mods—a failed mod should still be iterable, but what about one that failed before a repo was even created? Without a `repoDir`, the simplest honest approach is to just restart the full pipeline for that mod with the new prompt appended.

I'm deciding the cleanest way to represent this: `run(mod, turn)` should branch on whether `mod.repoDir` exists—if so, take the revise path; if not, treat it as a retry where the spec prompt combines all turn prompts joined together, essentially describing the mod's intent as the original request plus whatever follow-up text the user added.

For the revise path, I'm looking at the PHASES list in shared.jsx and figuring out which phases to skip—since the repo already exists, revision should go spec → build → compile → deploy → playtest → fix → done, bypassing the repo creation step, while still letting the phase index logic mark 'repo' as completed in the checklist. I'm planning a `specRevision({ mod, request })` function in prompts.cjs that reuses the same plan rules and output shape as the original spec step, and to avoid duplicating logic I want to refactor the shared rules and plan shape into constants that both `spec()` and `specRevision()` can reference.

The reviser prompt needs to tell the agent the mod already exists and describe the user's requested change, updated behavior, and new test plan, instructing it to modify the existing implementation while preserving what still works, then build without committing. I'm checking that the fixer prompt still works correctly against the updated spec and test plan after a failed revision attempt, that the test plan file gets rewritten and committed separately, that playtest attempt directories stay uniquely numbered across the whole run, and that the seeded-attempt logic only applies on the very first attempt of the initial run rather than during revisions where the first attempt is a 'reviser' role.

Now I need to add 'reviser' as a branch in the codePhase role dispatch alongside seeded/builder/fixer. For the attempt loop and messaging, I want attempt counts to reflect attempts within the current turn rather than across the mod's whole history, which means tracking which turn each attempt belongs to -- I'm leaning toward storing a `turn` index on each attempt, treating legacy attempts without one as turn 0, and adding a helper to pull attempts for just the latest turn for use in the UI.

I also need to check how InsightsPage and ModsPage compute first-try pass rates, since revisions will muddy mod-level stats that assume a single attempt sequence. For session lookup, `mod.sessions.find(s => s.role==='spec')` only grabs the first matching session, so with a revision adding a second spec session, both turns would incorrectly show the same session's metadata -- I need to tag sessions and feed entries with their turn index so lookups can disambiguate between the original and revision spec sessions.

I'm also considering whether the reviser agent should resume the original Claude session versus starting fresh with repo context plus checkpoints -- fresh seems sufficient. For persisted mods without a `turns` array, I need a normalization step on load that backfills a default initial turn entry, then I can define the turn and feed structure going forward: an array of turn records starting with the initial prompt, with subsequent entries appended on each revise.

On revise I push a new turn and feed a 'user' kind item with the prompt text, which the thread builder uses to render user bubbles -- the initial bubble is synthesized from the first turn's prompt rather than pulled from feed. Since the demo has no `studio:create`, I don't need to add `studio:revise` there, but since sample mods lack `turns`, the UI needs to tolerate `mod.turns` being undefined. I'll write a `turnsOf(mod)` helper that falls back to constructing a single-turn array from the mod's prompt and creation time when no turns exist.

For the Composer flow: when a mod exists, follow-ups call `studio:revise` instead of creating a new mod, skipping navigation since we're already on that mod's view, and revision updates flow through existing `studio:mod` events. I'm also updating the placeholder text so that when the current mod is running, it tells the user to wait for the build to finish rather than suggesting they describe the next one, while out-of-scope ideas like steering a running build get set aside for now.

Moving to backend work, I'm restructuring mods so each one represents a single chat thread: the first turn builds the plugin, and later turns revise it in place, which means adding a `turns` array to new mods and normalizing legacy mods on load to synthesize that same structure from their original prompt. I'm deciding the backend doesn't actually need to track per-attempt turn numbers since only the UI reads that value, so I'll just have the UI default missing values to 0 rather than duplicating that normalization logic on the backend.

For legacy mods that get revised, I need to snapshot their current test plan checks and summary into turn zero before overwriting them, so I'm adding that fallback logic inside the revise function, and planning to record each turn's checks/summary right after the spec phase runs. I'm also planning to track a per-turn status (passed/failed/stopped) alongside the overall mod status, which means restructuring the run function to use a shared finish helper that sets both.

Now I'm sketching out the actual run function: it grabs the latest turn, determines if this is a revision based on whether a repo directory already exists, sets up the active tracking object, starts the game if needed, clears any previous error, and then branches into either a fresh spec phase or a revise-spec phase depending on whether this is a new mod or an update.

After the spec phase, it stores the spec and test plan on the mod, updates the turn with a summary and checks, feeds the plan to the client, and then either creates a new repo for a brand-new mod or writes an updated test-plan.json and commits it with an "Update the in-game test plan" message for revisions. I'm weighing whether that commit should happen before the code-generation phase runs, matching the original flow's ordering.

I'm also handling the edge case where a previous turn's build died before a repo was ever created -- in that case it should fall back to the full non-revising pipeline, joining all the turn prompts together into one combined request since nothing was actually built yet.

For a seeded mod that fails before repo creation and then gets a follow-up turn, the spec phase will just re-use the seeded fixture and ignore the new prompt text, which is an acceptable edge case for now.

The builder currently only uses the single mod.prompt field, but for the retry-with-multiple-turns case it really needs the full joined request instead -- I'm considering whether to add a helper that joins all turn prompts and feed that into the builder prompt function, keeping in mind that normalized mods always have a turns array by the time they reach the backend.

I think the cleanest fix is to define a `userRequest(mod)` helper in prompts.cjs and export it so index.cjs can reuse the same logic for spec generation.

On the UI side, the phase list still includes a 'repo' step even during revisions where it's skipped, so I need to make sure that step doesn't get misleadingly marked as "done" -- instead I want to mark it as something like "Already set up" when revising. I'm thinking of tagging the turn itself with a `revision: true` flag when the repo already existed, rather than trying to infer it from the turn index, since a no-repo retry could still have a nonzero turn index while actually creating the repo fresh. I also want to adjust the step detail text so phases like "spec" and "build" show revision-specific language, e.g. "Update the spec and test plan for your change" instead of the first-run wording.

For the reviser agent's role, rather than introducing a brand-new 'reviser' role that would need its own avatar and CSS styling, I think it's simpler to keep using the existing 'builder' role for revision attempts and just add a separate `revision: true` flag on the attempt object. That way all the existing UI logic -- role labels, avatars, session lookups, code view, insights -- keeps working without changes, and I can just branch on `attempt.revision` wherever I need different prompt text (like picking `prompts.reviser` instead of the normal builder prompt).

Now I'm looking at how this affects the Insights page -- since attempts.length can now span multiple turns for multi-turn mods, metrics like "first try passed" or the attempts-to-pass histogram would get skewed if I don't scope them per-turn rather than across the whole attempt history. I realize the "first try" calculation breaks once revisions are added, since attempts.length would be 2+ for a mod revised on turn 2. I need to redefine attempts for the Insights metrics to only count attempts from the initial turn, filtering by turn 0.

But that creates a mismatch with status, which reflects the latest turn — a mod could fail turn 0 but pass after revision, making "attempts to pass" misleading if tied to turn 0 alone. I think the cleaner fix is to use attempts from whichever turn the mod's current status reflects (the latest turn), so firstTry/attemptsToPass/avgAttempts stay consistent with pass/fail status — I'll build a shared helper to pull attempts from the relevant turn.

Beyond the Insights tweak, I don't need to overhaul much else: ModsPage's total attempts count and spec/prompt display can stay as-is, ResultCard and the sidebar title are fine, though "Build plan" header should say "Change plan" for revisions. Now I'm moving into prompts.cjs to refactor the spec constants and add a revision-specific prompt.

Writing the spec revision prompt...

I can parametrize the max checks allowed, letting revisions go slightly higher than the initial plan.

I should also consider that users might ask pure questions rather than request changes, but since one chat represents one mod, I'll treat every message as implying a change rather than handling Q&A separately—that's out of scope for now.

Now I'm sketching the reviser prompt, which tells the agent to treat the mod as already existing and edit it based on the user's change request, referencing the mod's spec, prior turns, and the updated playtest plan, then build and summarize without committing.

I'm also noting that the revision spec phase runs in a separate studio directory outside the repo, calling the spec agent with no tools and parsing its JSON output to get the revised spec.

Since specPhase and revisionSpecPhase share so much validation logic, I'm thinking about merging them into a single function that branches on whether this is a revision — picking the right prompt, keeping the mod name consistent, and validating that the test plan has checks before returning the parsed spec.

I'm also tracing through edge cases: the agent call pushes onto mod.sessions regardless, a stopped session throws correctly, and a retried mod without a repo still correctly replaces its name from the new spec attempt.

I'm restructuring the attempt numbering so the loop starts from the last recorded attempt plus one, and reworking runAttempt to derive whether it's a first attempt directly from whether a previous attempt was passed in, which determines the role assigned and the phase label used.

I'm also refining commit messages to vary by role and revision status, including a short truncated snippet of the turn's prompt for readability when it's a revision, so the fixer has useful context from history.

For the builder's code phase, I'm selecting between the reviser prompt and the regular builder prompt depending on whether it's a revision, pulling the relevant turn's prompt as the request. I'm also defining a helper that concatenates all prior turn prompts into a single request string, so retries fold in new messages alongside the original ask.

I'm adding a small settle helper to set both module and turn status together on pass, fail, or stop, and working out how to phrase the final summary message based on how many attempts it took to succeed.

Now I'm writing the revise function: validate the mod exists, apply the same guards as create, stop any running demo, check the prompt is long enough, and detect whether this is a revision by checking if a repo already exists.

I'm considering whether to include failure context in the reviser's prompt, like noting the previous attempt's status or failure summary so the reviser agent understands what needs fixing.

I'm also checking whether legacy mod turns need their snapshot backfilled with spec summary and test checks when they lack them, though that patch may only be relevant to older mod structures rather than the normal flow.

Rather than special-casing this in revise(), it's cleaner to handle it in load()'s normalization step — defaulting mod.turns to a single legacy-derived turn with prompt, timestamp, summary, checks, terminal status, and revision flag set to false, plus defaulting attempts to zero if missing. I also need to make sure that if mod.status gets normalized from a non-terminal state like 'running' to 'stopped' during load, the corresponding turn.status reflects that same correction rather than staying undefined.

For pushing a new turn on revision, I'm adding it with the prompt text, timestamp, and revision flag, feeding a user message into the conversation, then setting mod.status and mod.phase to 'queued' so the UI immediately reflects pending work, mirroring how create() behaves before run() flips it to 'running'. I'm leaving turn.status unset at creation time since the UI reads live mod state for the latest turn rather than the turn's own status field, then proceeding to save the mod, emit the studio:mod event, trigger run(), and return the public mod.

I'm now worried about ordering and data loss: the feed cap that trims entries once they exceed 1500 could drop early 'user' feed items from earlier turns in long conversations, which would desync the turn index the UI derives by counting user feed items -- if early ones get dropped, later turns would be mislabeled. I should fix this by explicitly storing the turn index on each feed item (`turn: mod.turns.length`) rather than inferring it by position.

To avoid a naming collision between the existing 'turn' variable used for agent-turn grouping and my chat-turn index, I'll rename the latter to something like 'round' in the thread-building logic.

Writing thread item construction...

Still mapping feed items...

Simplifying by storing the resolved text directly on the item rather than reconstructing it from turns, with a fallback for synthetic feed entries. Still working out the plan card rendering...

Still determining frozen failure status...

I realize setPhase('done') actually fires on the failure path too, so phase lands at index 7 regardless—meaning for a failed turn, all steps before index 7 should render as done and the final step as failed.

For the stopped/catch path, I should instead store the phase at the moment of settling as `turn.endPhase`, then derive the frozen checklist state from that stored phase rather than live state. This lets me unify the logic so PipelineChecklist can compute passed/failed/running/current from either the live module or the frozen turn snapshot.

Writing checklist derivation logic...

I need to make sure legacy turns get an `endPhase` set during load normalization, and handle the edge case where it's undefined by letting phaseIndex default to -1 so everything shows as todo. I also need to handle the revision case where the repo step gets marked skipped with a "Already set up" label.

Now I'm turning to TestPlanChecklist — it needs to figure out which turn is the latest, pull the checks for that turn or fall back to the plan's checks, and determine the verdict from that turn's attempts specifically rather than globally. I'm realizing `latestVerdict` needs a turn-scoped variant, since the stale-verdict bug I found earlier (a new turn showing the previous turn's verdict before any attempt exists) stems from the test panel using the unscoped global latest verdict instead of filtering by the current turn's attempts.

I'll change latestVerdict so it only searches for a verdict within the given turn's attempts (defaulting to the latest turn), ensuring verdicts never leak across turns since a new turn's plan replaces the old one. Checking the Dock usage confirms it still works correctly with this default.

For legacy mods without a `turn` field on attempts, I treat them as turn 0, and for mods without a `turns` array I fall back to a synthetic single-turn structure built from the mod's own prompt and creation date, so `turnsOf` and `turnAttempts` stay consistent for old data.

Looking at `ResultCard`, it filters attempts for the current turn and counts lessons, with its messaging and check counts scoped per-turn while spend totals reflect the whole mod. I'm checking when it actually renders -- only at the end when the mod isn't running and has a terminal status -- so past turns don't get their own result card, just the phase "done" line, which raises the question of whether they should.

I realize there's a mismatch: seeded turn 0 has no spec session since there's no spec agent for it, so when I try to index into `sessions.filter(spec)` by turn number for the revision pass, the indices shift off by one and don't line up. The fix is to tag each spec session explicitly with its turn index when it's created in `agent()`, rather than relying on positional filtering.

With that sorted, I move to the Composer: `revising` is true when there's an existing module, and `canStart` requires either a non-empty prompt (at least 8 characters) or, if not revising, a seed value as an alternative starting point.

The start handler calls either "studio:revise" or "studio:create" depending on whether a module exists, clearing the prompt afterward. I also need to handle the `seed` disabling behavior so it only applies when there's no module, and adjust placeholder/hint/button text depending on whether the build is running, revising an existing mod, or starting fresh.

I'm also thinking through the edge case where a mod failed before getting a repoDir — in that case the placeholder should prompt the user to add detail and retry rather than referencing a mod name. I don't think a per-mod draft needs persisting, and the Welcome examples flow should stay unaffected; I'm now considering how typing into a mod chat should trigger a revision of that same mod.

For "New mod" clicks, composing becomes true and mod is null, triggering a create. After `studio:create` resolves, the app watches the newly created mod, sets composing false, and selects it — that's already correct and fixes the issue where later messages should route to revise instead of create.

I want to generalize the main.cjs wrapper so both `studio:create` and `studio:revise` get guarded through the same handler-wrapping loop, rather than duplicating logic. I also want to check whether `docs/hackathon/CONTRACTS.md` already documents these studio channels, since it looks like it's been modified outside this change.

The demo bridge lacks `studio:create`, so I don't need a revise handler, but demo mods have no `turns` and the UI must handle that gracefully. I'll now check the docs for studio channels and how `.role-avatar` CSS is keyed.

I notice the call used `studio:revise` rather than `studio:create`, which explains why the sidebar still shows one mod with two bubbles in the same thread. The status mismatch is confusing me - it shows "Passed" at the 3-second mark even though the simulated run should still be mid-process, which suggests the mock is mutating a shared status object that gets cloned on emit rather than tracking state per call.

Since enough time has likely elapsed for the whole 6-second simulation to complete, I should stop trying to infer the intermediate state and instead take a snapshot now to confirm the final result, then trigger another revise and sample the state at timed intervals to actually catch it mid-run.

content.thinking:
I'm checking the mid-run state: the header shows "Running," composer locked, send disabled, one mod active in the sidebar, and three bubbles with the plan updating live—step 2 of 8, repo skipped, build active—while the previous turn's plan stays frozen. Right after sending, the dock briefly showed a queued state before progressing to step 0 of 8 with attempt tracking and check counts.

I'm tracing the root cause: the dock logic uses `mod.attempts.at(-1)`, which pulls stale data from the previous turn's last attempt during the queued/spec phase of a new turn—for fresh mods this isn't an issue since attempts are empty, but for revisions it inherits the old attempt's start time and step label. The fix is to switch to `turnAttempts(mod).at(-1)` and derive the "since" timestamp from the current turn's start rather than the stale previous attempt, while leaving the existing pre-spec queued display for new mods alone since that part behaves correctly. I'm now working out exactly how to wire `since` and the attempt reference through `turnAttempts` in the dock component.

Mid-run looks correct overall, but I found a glitch: right after sending, the dock briefly shows the previous turn's last attempt ("attempt 3 · 22s") because `Dock` uses `mod.attempts.at(-1)` without scoping to the current turn. I'll fix this by scoping the attempt lookup to the current turn.

content.text:
A follow-up message in an open mod's chat now changes that same mod instead of starting a new one. All 31 tests pass and the frontend builds. I couldn't run the real Claude, Maven and Paper pipeline here. I tested the real `studio/index.cjs` with those stubbed, and drove the real UI against a fake backend.

## The cause
`Composer` in `BuildPage.jsx` always called `studio:create`, even with a mod open. The backend had no way to continue a mod.

## What changed
- **A mod is now a series of turns.** The first turn builds it, and each later message is another turn on the same repo. Attempt numbers keep counting up across turns.
- **Follow-ups edit the existing plugin.** A new `studio:revise` channel asks the spec agent to update the existing spec and test plan, keeping the same plugin name. A builder then edits the code in place, and it is compiled, deployed and playtested again. The fixer still gets up to 3 attempts per turn.
- **The UI renders one chat.** Each turn gets its own message, plan checklist and test plan. Earlier turns stay frozen at their own result.
- **Composer states.**
  - With a mod open, the placeholder reads "Ask for a change to SkyBlade…" and the Seeded-bug toggle is hidden.
  - While a build runs, the box is locked.
  - "New mod" (sidebar or chat header) is the way to start a separate mod.
- **Smaller adjustments:**
  - The dock, result card and Insights count only the latest turn's attempts.
  - The stale-code guard in `main.cjs` now covers `studio:revise`.
  - Mods saved before this change open as one-turn chats.

## Behaviour you might not assume
- **Every message is a change request.** A question like "why did it fail?" would still trigger a rebuild.
- **Failed first build:** if it died before creating a repo, your next message is folded into the original request and the build starts over.

New test: `tests/studio-turns.test.cjs`. I haven't committed anything. `studio/index.cjs` also contains your earlier uncommitted demo/reset work, so you'll want to review the diff before committing.
